title: One More Plague: The Death of the Firstborn Announced
summary: God tells Moses that one final plague will make Pharaoh drive Israel out, and that the Israelites should ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold. Moses announces to Pharaoh that at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's heir to the son of the lowest servant, while not even a dog will snarl at Israel. He leaves Pharaoh hot with anger, and the narrator sums up the plagues: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders, but the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart.
story: Chapter 11 is a hinge. The nine plagues of chapters 7 to 10 are over, and the Passover and the exodus of chapter 12 have not yet begun. In between, the last blow is announced. It is the one God warned about before the contest started, when he told Moses to say to Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son” (4:22), and that if Pharaoh would not release God's son, his own firstborn would die. Pharaoh had ordered Israel's sons thrown into the Nile (1:22); now the judgment turns back on Egypt's sons. The chapter also prepares for the departure itself, with the command to ask for silver and gold that God first gave at the burning bush (3:21-22). Verses 9 and 10 close the plague cycle by repeating what God said at its start: Pharaoh will not listen, so that God's wonders may be multiplied.
historical:
The phrases in verse 5 cover the whole of Egyptian society, from “the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne” to “the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill.” Grinding grain by hand, kneeling at a stone quern and pushing a smaller stone back and forth over it, was daily drudgery assigned to the lowest household servants, and Egyptian figurines show women at exactly that work. The firstborn of Pharaoh was the crown prince, the heir to a throne regarded as divine. No Egyptian record mentions such a catastrophe, which is not surprising given that Egyptian royal texts did not record defeats, and attempts to match it with the deaths of particular princes known from Egyptian history remain speculation.

The request for silver and gold (verse 2) fulfills what God told Abraham, that his descendants would come out of their slavery “with many possessions” (Genesis 15:14). The goods would later have a mixed history. The people gave gold for the tabernacle (35:22), but gold earrings taken from Egypt also went into the golden calf (32:2-4). The treasure of Egypt could serve the worship of the LORD or be turned into an idol.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East the firstborn son was the family's heir and the sign of its future, and in Egypt the king's firstborn stood for the continuity of the dynasty and of the order the gods maintained. The last plague strikes every household at its point of greatest hope. The phrase in verse 7, “not even a dog will snarl,” is literally that not a dog will sharpen its tongue, an idiom for complete calm. On the night when every Egyptian house is wailing, Israel's houses will be so undisturbed that not even a dog barks.

The command to ask for silver and gold has sometimes been misunderstood. Older English translations said the Israelites borrowed the goods, which made them look dishonest, but the Hebrew verb simply means to ask, and the text says the Egyptians granted the request because the LORD gave Israel favor with them (verse 3). Many readers see it as overdue wages for generations of unpaid labor. Israel's later law required masters who freed a slave not to send him away empty-handed but to furnish him liberally, and it grounds the command in this very memory: “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 15:13-15).
literary: The chapter's arrangement is unusual. Chapter 10 ended with Pharaoh banishing Moses and Moses agreeing never to see his face again, yet in verses 4 to 8 Moses is still speaking to Pharaoh. Most readers take verses 1 to 3 as a parenthesis, telling what God had already said to Moses, and verses 4 to 8 as the rest of Moses' final speech in that same audience; only in verse 8 does he finally leave. Several threads are tied off here. The great cry that will go up from Egypt (verse 6) uses the same Hebrew word as Israel's cry under slavery, which God heard at the bush (3:7, 9), so the oppressor now cries as the oppressed once did. The distinction God has made between Israel and Egypt since the flies (8:22-23) is stated for the last time, “the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel” (verse 7). And the summary in verses 9 and 10 echoes 7:3-4, where God first said he would multiply his signs and wonders and that Pharaoh would not listen. The whole plague cycle is framed by that promise and its fulfillment.

outline.t: One more plague, and silver and gold from the Egyptians
Moses announces the death of every firstborn
The wonders multiplied and Pharaoh's heart hardened

doctrines.note: The last plague is the most severe and the most deliberate. It was warned of before the first plague (4:23), it answers Pharaoh's own murder of Israel's sons, and it is announced again before it falls. In Scripture God's judgment is never random; it comes with warning, and it matches the wrong it answers.

God gives Israel favor with the Egyptians and makes Moses highly regarded among Pharaoh's own officials and people (verse 3). Even in the land of their enemies, God shapes the attitudes of others to provide for his people as he promised.

“The LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel” (verse 7). The distinction is not that Israel is better or innocent, as the next chapter shows by requiring the blood of a lamb for Israel's houses too. It is God's choice to claim and protect a people for himself.

words.note: Tse'aqah, a cry or outcry, especially the cry of those in distress. God heard Israel's cry in Egypt (3:7, 9). Now, in verse 6, a great cry will go up from all Egypt, one never heard before or since. The word ties the last plague to the beginning of the story: the oppressor comes to share the anguish he caused.

Palah, to be distinct or set apart. God uses it in verse 7 for the distinction he makes between Egypt and Israel, as he did with the flies (8:22) and the livestock (9:4). The same verb appears when Moses later asks how anyone will know that God is with Israel unless his presence sets them apart from every other people (33:16).

Chen, favor or grace, the goodwill that one person shows another. The LORD gives his people favor in the sight of the Egyptians (verse 3). It is the word used when Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8), and it reminds the reader that Israel's goods on leaving Egypt were a gift, not a theft.

Mophet, a wonder or portent, an extraordinary event that points to God's power. It often appears with the word for sign, as in signs and wonders. Verses 9 and 10 use it to sum up all the plagues, which Moses and Aaron performed before Pharaoh so that God's wonders might be multiplied in Egypt.

christ: The death of Egypt's firstborn and the sparing of Israel's firstborn stand behind some of the New Testament's deepest language about Jesus. He is called God's Son, and Paul calls him “firstborn from among the dead” (Colossians 1:18), the first to rise into the new creation. In Exodus, God struck the firstborn of Egypt and spared the firstborn of Israel. In the gospel, the Father “did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Paul's wording there echoes Abraham and Isaac more than Exodus, but the pattern of the two stories meets at the cross: the firstborn of God dies so that others will be spared. Hebrews extends the title to believers, calling the church “the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven” (Hebrews 12:23), a people who share the status of God's firstborn because of the One who went through death for them.

hard.q: How can a just God kill the firstborn children of Egypt?
hard.a:
This is the hardest moment in the plague story, and the text does not soften it. It announces the death of every firstborn, from the palace to the servant's quarters, and it records the great cry that follows. Readers who doubt the events happened as told still face the question of what the story says about God.

Several things are said in response. The first is that the judgment answers a crime. Pharaoh had ordered the killing of Israel's newborn sons (1:16, 22), and God warned him before the first plague that his refusal to release God's firstborn would cost him his own (4:22-23). Nine plagues and months of warnings came first. The second is that Scripture presents God, the giver of life, as having an authority over life and death that no human possesses: “I bring death and I give life” (Deuteronomy 32:39). The Bible never offers this plague as a model for human violence. The third is that Israel's firstborn were not spared for being innocent. They too were under the sentence and were protected only by the blood of the Passover lamb (12:13), and afterward God claimed them as his own (13:2). Christians add that the story does not end with God demanding the firstborn of others, but with God giving up his own Son. None of these answers removes the grief of the text. They set it inside a story in which God takes evil seriously, judges it justly, and provides at his own cost a way of escape.

questions: The cry of Egypt in verse 6 echoes the cry of Israel that God heard in chapter 3. What does it mean for you that God hears the cry of the oppressed and does not forget it?

Israel was to leave Egypt not empty-handed but with the Egyptians' silver and gold. How does Israel's later law about freeing slaves (Deuteronomy 15:13-15) shape the way you think about generosity toward people who have worked for you?
Moses left Pharaoh “hot with anger” after announcing the final judgment. When is anger at stubborn evil a right response, and how do you keep it from turning into something else?
